blocks.text: How can we express statements like 'Every student in the class passed the exam' using formal logic? This lesson introduces quantifiers, which allow us to make such statements precisely.

blocks.markdown: In predicate logic, quantifiers are symbols that allow us to express statements about 'all' or 'some' elements in a domain. The two primary quantifiers are the universal quantifier (∀) and the existential quantifier (∃).

blocks.title: Universal Quantifier
blocks.text: The universal quantifier (∀) is used to state that a property holds for all elements in a domain. For example, ∀x P(x) means 'for all x, P(x) is true.'

blocks.title: Existential Quantifier
blocks.text: The existential quantifier (∃) is used to state that there exists at least one element in a domain for which a property holds. For example, ∃x P(x) means 'there exists an x such that P(x) is true.'

blocks.markdown: Variables in logical expressions can be either **free** or **bound**. A variable is bound if it is within the scope of a quantifier; otherwise, it is free.

blocks.title: Bound and Free Variables
blocks.text: A variable is bound if it is quantified by a universal or existential quantifier. A variable is free if it is not within the scope of any quantifier.

blocks.title: Identifying Free and Bound Variables
blocks.prompt: Consider the expression ∀x (P(x) ∧ ∃y Q(y, x)). Identify the free and bound variables.

steps.text: First, identify the scope of each quantifier. The scope of ∀x is the entire expression P(x) ∧ ∃y Q(y, x).
Within the scope of ∀x, x is a bound variable. The scope of ∃y is Q(y, x), so y is bound within Q(y, x).
Since both x and y are within the scope of quantifiers, there are no free variables in this expression.

blocks.answer: There are no free variables; x and y are both bound.

blocks.markdown: The order of quantifiers can significantly affect the meaning of a logical expression. Consider the difference between ∀x ∃y P(x, y) and ∃y ∀x P(x, y).

blocks.title: Effect of Quantifier Order
blocks.prompt: Translate the following English sentences into logical expressions and explain the difference: (1) 'For every student, there is a book they like.' (2) 'There is a book that every student likes.'

steps.text: Translate (1): 'For every student, there is a book they like.' This becomes ∀x ∃y Likes(x, y), where x represents students and y represents books.
Translate (2): 'There is a book that every student likes.' This becomes ∃y ∀x Likes(x, y).
In (1), each student may like a different book. In (2), there is one specific book that all students like.

blocks.answer: Expression (1) is ∀x ∃y Likes(x, y); expression (2) is ∃y ∀x Likes(x, y). The order of quantifiers changes the meaning.

blocks.title: Quantifier Order
blocks.text: The order of quantifiers is crucial. ∀x ∃y P(x, y) is not equivalent to ∃y ∀x P(x, y).

points: Quantifiers allow us to express statements about all or some elements in a domain.
Variables can be free or bound, depending on their relation to quantifiers.
The order of quantifiers affects the meaning of logical expressions.
